source.title: Effective Regularization Through Evolutionary Loss-Function Metalearning
source.authors: Santiago Gonzalez; Xin Qiu; Risto Miikkulainen

record.file_problem: Full text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results on loss-function regularization and generalization, including a stated qualification that its experiments do not compare different regularization methods. Its results bear on the claim's broad relation between regularization and generalization, but do not directly test V1–V8 as written.
record.gate_note: The study measures attraction toward zero training error during training and reports test-set accuracy for TaylorGLO loss functions with and without a search constraint. It does not measure the training–test gap or test the claim versions' specific interventions or properties. The cited prior-work claims in the introduction, appendices and figure captions are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes TaylorGLO training dynamics and evaluates loss-function search and adversarial robustness. None of its own results tests V1–V8. Its filter-normalized accuracy-basin plots do not measure magnitude-aware training-error sharpness against training–test gaps or compare generalization measures, as V7 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors interpret TaylorGLO as balancing fitting against overconfidence, show that its parameterization can represent label smoothing, and propose this as groundwork for a broader theory. They report improved search results for AlexNet and AllCNN-C, no significant improvement for PreResNet-20, and increased FGSM robustness that can be enhanced through an adversarial evolution objective.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and experimentally evaluates evolutionary loss-function metalearning, rather than directly testing the claim versions' interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The TaylorGLO invariant constraint produced differing test accuracies across the three reported CIFAR-10 architectures; the authors state the constraint never had a detrimental effect in many cases, aside from greater computational cost, while the PreResNet-20 comparison had p-value 0.2827.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-entropy continually attracts samples toward confident correct predictions; TaylorGLO initially attracts samples and later repels most highly learned samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Evolved loss functions can implement a push–pull training dynamic that discourages overconfidence.

fits_no_version.finding: Invariant-constrained search with population 40 improves mean test accuracy for AlexNet and AllCNN-C relative to unconstrained search with population 20; PreResNet-20 has a small, non-significant decrease.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The combined invariant-filtering and larger-population search recipe can improve discovered loss functions on some CIFAR-10 architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 6 shows a wider, flatter filter-normalized accuracy basin for adversarially evolved TaylorGLO than standard TaylorGLO despite equal unperturbed accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-function evolution can increase parameter-perturbation tolerance without increasing unperturbed accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (2025 shorter version; supplied metadata lists IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation, 2020)
record.problems: The text says the paper does not aim to compare regularization methods. The reported empirical generalization results concern TaylorGLO search, not direct measurements of training–test gaps. Figure 5 and Figure 6 results are plots without tabulated numeric values and concern adversarial robustness, outside the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 and Figure 6 report adversarial robustness and loss-surface visualizations, which do not measure any claim version's behavior. Cited prior results, including TaylorGLO generalization improvements from earlier work, were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting capacity and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers, including local connectivity and transferred initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Do not assign T5 merely because the study concerns regularization: it does not qualify or contradict a listed version. Figure 4 reports ten separately trained models per condition, standard deviations, and one-tailed Welch tests. Figure 6 concerns accuracy under parameter perturbations, not the training–test-gap relationship in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and held-out performance.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects and interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removal of memorized training examples and resulting test accuracy.
